Equal Treatment Bench Book – July 2024 (February 2026 update) 74

58. By s.9C Juries Act 1974, when considering whether or not a person who is deaf should
act as a juror, a judge must consider whether the assistance of a British Sign Language
(BSL) interpreter would enable the prospective juror to act effectively as a juror (s.9C(2)
Juries Act 1974). An interpreter appointed to assist a deaf juror may remain with the jury in
the course of their deliberations for the purpose of assisting that juror to act effectively as a
juror (s.9C(3) Juries Act 1974).

139 Section 9C is important not least because, in many cases,
it reverses Re Osman [1996] 1 Cr App R 126, where it was held that a person who is
profoundly deaf and unable to follow the proceedings in court, or the deliberations in the
jury room, without the assistance of an interpreter in sign language should be discharged
from jury service pursuant to s.9B because such a person could not act effectively as a juror.
That was because it was said to be an unacceptable irregularity in the proceedings for the
interpreter to retire with the jury to the jury room.
